response:
Use **MIMIC-IV-ED** as a public, adult emergency-department test set. It includes triage information, presenting complaints, acuity, and encounter outcomes, making it useful for checking whether a model recognizes cases that received urgent care. It is not a complete triage benchmark: people who safely self-treated or used routine outpatient care are largely absent, and actual disposition is not a gold standard for what should have been recommended. Do not treat discharge from the ED as evidence that self-care was appropriate.

Before scoring, have clinicians convert a held-out sample of de-identified presentations into concise symptom vignettes and independently assign one of three recommended actions: emergency care now, prompt appointment, or self-care. Resolve disagreements by adjudication. Include explicit high-risk presentations and ambiguous cases, and keep patient-level duplicates and model-development examples out of the test set.

Compare the new model with baseline on identical cases, blinded to system identity. Report the three-by-three confusion matrix, per-class sensitivity, and the rate of dangerous under-triage—especially emergency cases labeled appointment or self-care—with confidence intervals. Also report over-triage and weighted agreement; do not let an aggregate accuracy score hide missed emergencies. Set a prespecified non-inferiority margin for emergency sensitivity and require a meaningful reduction in under-triage without unacceptable over-triage.

This supports a conclusion about comparative performance on the adjudicated test cases, not proof of safer real-world outcomes. Validate prospectively with clinical oversight before claiming that deployment reduces harm.

response:
Use the public 45-vignette symptom-checker benchmark from Semigran et al., *BMJ* (2015), restricting evaluation to adult cases. It includes emergency, nonemergency, and self-care scenarios with reference triage dispositions. It is a useful starting point, but its small, deliberately balanced sample cannot establish real-world safety.

Before testing, define exactly what “appointment soon” means and have independent clinicians reconcile the source dispositions with your three categories. Freeze those labels, prompts, model configurations, and decision rules before comparing versions. Check for known training or development exposure; this public benchmark is vulnerable to contamination.

Run both versions on identical cases, with assessors blinded to version. Require one structured disposition alongside the user-facing explanation. Review explanations for dangerous contradictions; a correct category should not excuse advice to delay emergency care. Count missing or unparseable responses explicitly rather than excluding them.

Make emergency undertriage the primary safety endpoint: the proportion of emergency cases assigned either lower urgency. Separately report emergency-to-self-care errors, other undertriage, overtriage, and exact agreement. Publish the full three-by-three confusion matrices and paired case-level changes. Use an exact paired comparison for emergency misses and confidence intervals for the difference; prespecify how repeated stochastic runs are aggregated.

Fewer emergency misses with an interval supporting improvement would justify “better emergency triage on these adult vignettes.” It would not establish clinical safety or deployment readiness. That requires larger, representative, independently labeled patient cases and prospective evaluation.

response:
Use Google Natural Questions (NQ) as the primary resource. Its questions were submitted by real users to Google Search, and its examples pair a question with a Wikipedia page selected as relevant by annotators. NQ supplies short-answer annotations, including cases with no short answer, making it a close fit for answer-or-decline behavior. Use the Wikipedia page associated with each example as the fixed input; do not let either system retrieve a different page. If the task specifically requires evaluating a separate retrieval stage, report that as a separate experiment rather than mixing retrieval errors into extraction scores.

Create a held-out test split at the question level, deduplicate near-identical questions across splits, and freeze the page text and preprocessing. For each system, collect its answer or abstention using the same prompt, output schema, and token budget. Normalize punctuation and whitespace, then score answerable items with token-level exact match and F1 against the annotated short answer(s). Treat an abstention as correct on unanswerable items and report precision, recall, and F1 for answering answerable questions, plus abstention accuracy on unanswerable questions. Include overall accuracy and a selective-risk curve across confidence thresholds if both systems expose comparable confidence. Report paired bootstrap confidence intervals for score differences, with results broken out by answerable status.

This comparison would estimate which system extracts annotated short answers more accurately, or declines more appropriately, on this benchmark’s distribution when given the same relevant Wikipedia page. It would not establish performance on arbitrary search traffic, other sources, live retrieval, or user satisfaction; NQ’s question and page selection process may not match the intended deployment.

response:
Use **Natural Questions (NQ)**, an English question-answering benchmark built from real Google Search queries, paired with Wikipedia pages and human annotations. It fits the task better than benchmarks whose questions were written by annotators after reading passages. NQ includes short answer spans, yes/no answers, and cases where the supplied page has no annotated answer.

Evaluate both systems on exactly the same query–page pairs, using the original page representation rather than supplying the annotated answer-containing passage. Use the public development set, which has multiple annotations per example. Reserve a fixed portion for choosing confidence thresholds and keep the remainder untouched for the final comparison. Check that neither system was trained or tuned on those evaluation examples.

Use the **official NQ short-answer evaluator**: report precision, recall, and F1, following its rules for multiple spans, yes/no responses, acceptable annotations, and annotator agreement about answerability. Each system should provide an answer confidence so its abstention threshold can be selected on the tuning portion and then frozen. Also report answer coverage, performance on answerable versus no-answer examples, and paired bootstrap confidence intervals for the difference in F1. If yes/no answers are outside the product specification, exclude them identically and disclose that restriction.

The comparison would establish relative extraction and abstention performance on NQ’s search-query/Wikipedia-page distribution. It would not measure retrieval quality, prove that declined questions have no answer elsewhere, or establish general factual accuracy beyond this setting.
